I10.overview: A condition characterised by elevated blood pressure measured on 3 separate occasions, a minimum of 2 days apart: systolic BP ≥ 140 mmHg and/or diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg.
phases: Step 1 — Lifestyle modification (3 months trial if no risk factors)
Step 2 — Add thiazide/thiazide-like diuretic
Step 3 — Add second antihypertensive
Step 4 — Increase dose of second medicine
Step 5 — Add third antihypertensive
Step 6 — Increase dose of third medicine
Step 7 — Add fourth medicine (spironolactone) — refer if uncontrolled

medications.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
medications.notes: Thiazide diuretic. Contraindicated in gout, pregnancy, severe liver impairment, eGFR < 30 mL/min.

medications.name: Amlodipine
medications.notes: Long-acting calcium channel blocker. Avoid in untreated heart failure.

medications.name: Enalapril
medications.notes: ACE-inhibitor. Contraindicated in pregnancy, bilateral renal artery stenosis, aortic valve stenosis, history of angioedema, hyperkalaemia, eGFR < 30 mL/min.

medications.name: Spironolactone
medications.notes: Doctor-initiated only. Risk of severe hyperkalaemia — monitor serum potassium within 1 month of therapy and thereafter. Do NOT use with potassium supplements or NSAIDs.

lifestyleAdvice: Stop smoking
Maintain ideal weight (BMI 18–25 kg/m²)
Salt restriction — remove salt from table, reduce salt in cooking, avoid processed foods
Increase potassium intake from fresh fruits and vegetables
Reduce alcohol to ≤ 2 standard drinks/day for males, ≤ 1 for females
Follow a healthy eating plan (low fat, high fibre, unrefined carbohydrates)
Regular moderate aerobic exercise — 30 minutes brisk walking, 5–7 times/week

baseline: Serum potassium (if on ACE-inhibitor or eGFR < 30 mL/min)
sixMonthly: Serum potassium (if on spironolactone or eGFR < 30 mL/min)

I10.followUpSchedule: Monthly monitoring and therapy adjustment until BP is stable. Once target BP achieved, review every 3–6 months. If lifestyle modification alone, re-assess after 3 months.
warningSigns: Severe headache with blurred vision or confusion
Neurological signs — coma, seizures, visual disturbances
referralCriteria: BP not controlled on 4 medicines and no doctor available

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Systolic BP > 180 mmHg and/or diastolic BP > 130 mmHg WITH organ damage symptoms
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Amlodipine 10 mg oral as single dose. If pulmonary oedema: Furosemide 40 mg IV.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Life-threatening — needs immediate referral to hospital

specialCases.note: Initiate medicine treatment only when BP > 160/90 mmHg. Lower BP slowly over a few days.
See Section 6.4.2 — Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Do NOT treat elevated BP at PHC — refer urgently

I10.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 4, Section 4.7.1

E11.9.overview: A chronic metabolic disease characterised by hyperglycaemia with serious acute and chronic complications. Most adults with type 2 diabetes are overweight.

glycaemicTargets.patientType: Young, low risk / Newly diagnosed / No CVD

phases: Step 1 — Lifestyle modification + Metformin
Step 2 — Add sulphonylurea (if HbA1c not at target after 2–3 months)
Step 3 — Insulin therapy (doctor-initiated; stop sulphonylurea, continue metformin)

medications.name: Metformin
medications.frequency: Once daily with meals, titrate slowly
medications.notes: First-line agent. Contraindicated in uncontrolled congestive cardiac failure, severe liver disease, significant respiratory compromise, and renal impairment (eGFR < 30 mL/min).

medications.name: Gliclazide
medications.notes: Preferred sulphonylurea in the elderly. Only add if HbA1c > 8% despite 2–3 months of maximal metformin. Missing meals may cause hypoglycaemia.

medications.name: Insulin (Intermediate to long-acting)
medications.notes: Doctor-initiated. If 10 units ineffective, increase gradually to 20 units (2–4 unit increase per week). Continue metformin; STOP sulphonylurea when insulin is initiated.

lifestyleAdvice: Regular, evenly-spaced meals with small portions
Nutritionally balanced meals — one protein, one starch, two vegetables, one fruit, water
Strict carbohydrate control — favour whole grains, legumes, vegetables
Discourage processed/refined carbs (takeaways, cakes, white bread, sugary drinks)
Aim for 5 servings of fruit/vegetables per day; limit fruit to 2 servings/day
Prefer fat-free or low-fat dairy
Eat oily fish (sardines, pilchards) 2–3 times per week
Salt: do not exceed half a teaspoon per day
Increased physical activity — 30 minutes, 5 times a week
Appropriate weight loss if overweight
Stop smoking; limit alcohol
Foot care education — inspect feet daily
Wear a medical notification bracelet

portionGuide.protein: Size of your palm (about 90 g or ½ cup)
portionGuide.fruitsVegStarch: No larger than your clenched fist (1 cup)

E11.9.followUpSchedule: Review monthly until stable. Once at target, review every 3–6 months. HbA1c every 3–6 months while therapy changes. Annual comprehensive review.

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Altered level of consciousness, acidotic breathing, dehydration, ketonuria, or glucose > 25 mmol/L
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Check blood glucose and test urine for ketones. If diagnosis uncertain, treat as hypoglycaemia and refer urgently.

hypoglycaemiaTreatment.conscious: Sweets, sugar, glucose by mouth, OR oral sugar solution (3 tsp sugar in 200 mL water)
hypoglycaemiaTreatment.unconscious: Dextrose 10% IV, 2–5 mL/kg. Re-check glucose 10–15 min later.

E11.9.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 9, Section 9.2.2

B20.overview: HIV is a retrovirus that attacks the immune system, specifically CD4 lymphocytes. Without treatment it progressively destroys immunity, leading to opportunistic infections and AIDS. With effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), people living with HIV can achieve near-normal life expectancy. All PLHIV are eligible for ART, regardless of CD4 count or WHO stage.
phases: Diagnosis — confirm with 2 rapid tests from different manufacturers; do CD4 count and WHO staging
ART initiation — start TLD as soon as feasible, ideally same-day if patient is ready
Monitoring — VL at 3 & 10 months, then annually if suppressed
Long-term care — continued adherence support and viral suppression

medications.name: Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir (TLD)
medications.dosage: TDF 300 mg + 3TC 300 mg + DTG 50 mg (single tablet)
medications.notes: The preferred first-line regimen for all adults including women of child-bearing potential. Check creatinine before starting TDF — avoid TDF if eGFR <50 mL/min. If HBsAg positive, TDF must form part of the regimen.

medications.name: TDF + Emtricitabine + Efavirenz (TEE)
medications.dosage: TDF 300 mg + FTC 200 mg + EFV 600 mg
medications.phase: Alternative first-line — patients on rifampicin-based TB treatment who cannot use DTG
medications.notes: Used when patient is on rifampicin-based TB treatment and cannot double-dose DTG, or has DTG intolerance/contraindication.

medications.name: TDF + 3TC + DTG (with double-dose DTG)
medications.dosage: TDF 300 mg + 3TC 300 mg + DTG 50 mg twice daily
medications.duration: During TB treatment + 2 weeks after stopping rifampicin
medications.phase: Alternative — patients on rifampicin-based TB treatment
medications.notes: Rifampicin reduces DTG concentrations. Additional 50 mg DTG dose given 12 hours after the TLD dose.

medications.name: TDF + 3TC/FTC + Atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r)
medications.phase: Protease inhibitor-based regimen — contraindications to BOTH EFV and DTG
medications.notes: If patient requires rifampicin-based TB treatment, substitute ATV/r with LPV/r at 800/200 mg 12-hourly.

medications.name: Abacavir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir (ALD)
medications.phase: Alternative — TDF contraindication (eGFR <50 mL/min), no chronic hepatitis B
medications.notes: If chronic hepatitis B coinfection AND eGFR 30-50 mL/min, use TAF + FTC + DTG instead.

medications.name: Zidovudine + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir
medications.dosage: AZT 300 mg + 3TC 150 mg (twice daily) + DTG 50 mg daily
medications.frequency: AZT/3TC twice daily; DTG once daily
medications.phase: Alternative — intolerance to TDF/TAF and ABC
medications.notes: Monitor FBC at months 1 and 3 for AZT-related anaemia.

medications.name: Cotrimoxazole (OI prophylaxis)
medications.notes: Indicated for WHO stage 3/4 or CD4 <200.

medications.name: Isoniazid (TB Preventive Therapy)
medications.notes: Give to all adult PLHIV who don't have active TB, liver disease, or prior MDR/XDR-TB.

medications.name: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
medications.notes: Prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy.

lifestyleAdvice: Take your ART at the same time every day — adherence is essential
Never skip doses — resistance develops quickly from missed doses
Use condoms during sexual intercourse to prevent transmission and STIs
Disclose your HIV status to someone who can be your treatment supporter
Join a support or peer group for people living with HIV
Eat a balanced diet and maintain a healthy weight
Stop smoking and limit alcohol
Get your flu vaccine annually
Attend every clinic appointment
If you have TB symptoms, report them immediately

onART: Viral load at 3 and 10 months, then annually if suppressed
CD4 at 10 months; stop once >200 and suppressed
If on TDF: creatinine at month 3, month 10, annually
If on AZT: FBC at 1 and 3 months
Weight, blood pressure, adherence at every visit

B20.followUpSchedule: Viral load at 3 and 10 months after ART initiation and annually if suppressed. Clinical review at every script refill.
warningSigns: New cough lasting more than 2 weeks (possible TB)
Fever with night sweats and weight loss
Blurred vision or sudden vision changes
Severe diarrhoea lasting more than 2 weeks
New purple or dark skin patches (possible Kaposi's sarcoma)
referralCriteria: Virological failure on TLD >2 years with 2 consecutive VL ≥1000

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Fever + neck stiffness, altered consciousness, or severe dyspnoea in an HIV+ patient
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Assess ABCDE. Refer urgently for LP and CSF CrAg if meningitis signs. If suspected IRIS: assess, do not stop ART, refer.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Most HIV-related emergencies need hospital referral.

specialCases.note: Initiate ART immediately with TLD if no contraindication.
Start TB first. CD4 <50: ART within 2 weeks; CD4 ≥50: defer 8 weeks. Watch for IRIS.
Defer ART 8 weeks.
Defer ART 4-6 weeks after starting antifungals.

B20.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 11, Section 11.1

Z21.overview: A patient who has tested HIV-positive but has no current symptoms of HIV disease (WHO clinical stage 1). Despite being asymptomatic, ART should be initiated as soon as feasible.
phases: Confirm HIV-positive status — do CD4 count and baseline investigations
Start ART as soon as feasible
Monitor viral load — target undetectable
Lifelong adherence support

medications.name: Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir (TLD)
medications.notes: Same first-line regimen as for symptomatic HIV.

medications.name: Cotrimoxazole (prophylaxis — if indicated)
medications.notes: Only if CD4 <200 cells/mm³ or WHO stage 3/4.

lifestyleAdvice: Take your ART every day at the same time
Use condoms during sexual intercourse
Inform your sexual partners so they can be tested
Attend every clinic appointment
Maintain a healthy lifestyle
Get your annual flu vaccine
Report any new symptoms to your CHW or clinic promptly

baseline: Confirm HIV-positive status with 2 rapid tests
onART: Viral load at 3 and 10 months, then annually if suppressed
CD4 at 10 months (stop if >200 and suppressed)
Creatinine (if on TDF) at month 3, month 10, annually

Z21.followUpSchedule: Same as for symptomatic HIV — VL at 3 and 10 months, then annually if suppressed.
warningSigns: Weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, persistent fever
Swollen glands lasting more than a few weeks
referralCriteria: Any new symptoms suggesting WHO stage 2, 3, or 4 progression
Z21.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 11, Section 11.1

Z29.2.conditionName: HIV prophylaxis (cotrimoxazole and TB preventive therapy)
Z29.2.overview: Preventive treatment for people living with HIV to reduce the risk of opportunistic infections. Includes cotrimoxazole prophylaxis and TB Preventive Therapy (TPT) with isoniazid.
Z29.2.treatmentDurationText: Varies — cotrimoxazole until CD4 >200; TPT for 12 months
phases: Initiation — after excluding active infections
Maintenance — continued prophylaxis
Discontinuation — when criteria met

medications.name: Cotrimoxazole
medications.notes: Indicated for WHO Clinical stage 3 or 4, or CD4 <200 cells/mm³. Watch for maculopapular rash.

medications.name: Isoniazid (INH)
medications.notes: Give to all adult PLHIV. Exclude active TB first.

medications.name: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
medications.notes: Prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy.

lifestyleAdvice: Take your prophylaxis every day at the same time as your ART
Do not stop cotrimoxazole or isoniazid without telling your clinic
Report any new rash, tingling, or yellow eyes to your CHW immediately
Attend monthly check-ups for the first 3 months of TPT

everyVisit: Ask about tingling in hands/feet (isoniazid neuropathy)
Ask about nausea, vomiting, yellow eyes (isoniazid hepatotoxicity)
baseline: Exclude active TB before starting TPT

Z29.2.followUpSchedule: Cotrimoxazole: until CD4 >200. TPT: monthly for first 3 months, then routine; complete 12-month course.
warningSigns: New rash with fever or mucosal involvement
Nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite
Any TB symptom appearing while on prophylaxis

specialCases.note: Defer TPT until after delivery.
Do NOT use rifapentine-containing 3HP regimen.
Exclude from TPT.

Z29.2.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 11, Sections 11.2.1 and 11.2.2

A15.overview: Tuberculosis is an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, most commonly affecting the lungs. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. TB is a notifiable disease. Drug-sensitive TB is treated with a 6-month regimen: 2 months of intensive-phase RHZE followed by 4 months of continuation-phase RH.
phases: Intensive phase (Months 1–2) — RHZE 4-drug combination daily
Continuation phase (Months 3–6) — RH 2-drug combination daily
Cure — sputum smear-negative at month 5 or 6

medications.name: RHZE — Rifampicin + Isoniazid + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol (fixed-dose combination)
medications.frequency: Once daily, same time each day
medications.notes: The 4-in-1 tablet contains Rifampicin 150 mg + Isoniazid 75 mg + Pyrazinamide 400 mg + Ethambutol 275 mg. Take all tablets in ONE dose. Rifampicin may turn urine, sweat and tears orange — this is harmless. Rifampicin reduces the effectiveness of combined oral contraceptives — advise alternative contraception.

medications.name: RH — Rifampicin + Isoniazid (fixed-dose combination)
medications.frequency: Once daily, same time each day
medications.notes: Two formulations: RH 150/75 mg and RH 300/150 mg.

medications.name: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
medications.duration: Full duration of TB treatment (6 months)
medications.notes: Prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy.

lifestyleAdvice: Take all your TB tablets every day without missing any dose
Take all tablets together in ONE dose at the same time each day
Do not stop treatment even if you feel better — completing 6 months is essential
Cover your mouth when you cough or sneeze
Open windows and let in sunlight at home
Eat a nutritious, balanced diet
Stop smoking and avoid excessive alcohol
Attend every follow-up appointment, including sputum tests
Inform close contacts so they can be screened
Report immediately: yellow eyes/skin, dark urine, severe nausea, tingling, skin rash

everyVisit: Weight — adjust tablet count if weight changes
baseline: Sputum TB-NAAT — confirm TB and check for rifampicin resistance

A15.followUpSchedule: Monthly clinical review. Sputum smear at month 2, 5, 6. If smear positive at month 2, consider adherence and DR-TB. If positive at month 5/6, refer for treatment failure.
warningSigns: Severe nausea or vomiting with abdominal pain
New skin rash with fever or facial swelling
Severe chest pain or difficulty breathing
referralCriteria: Failure to convert to smear-negative at month 2 despite adherence
Treatment failure (positive smear at month 5 or 6)

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Signs of disseminated TB, TB meningitis, or severe adverse drug reaction
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Refer to hospital same day. For suspected TB meningitis: urgent LP. For suspected drug-induced hepatitis: STOP all TB medicines before referral.

specialCases.note: Treat TB and HIV. Start TB first, then add ART based on CD4. Rifampicin reduces DTG concentration — double DTG dose while on rifampicin.
Ethambutol and pyrazinamide three times weekly. Rifampicin and isoniazid do not require adjustment.
All first-line TB drugs are safe in pregnancy. Give pyridoxine 25 mg daily.
Stop all TB medicines, refer urgently for same-day ALT.
Rifampicin reduces efficacy of combined oral contraceptives. Advise IUD or DMPA.

A15.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 17, Sections 17.4.1 and 17.4.1.2

A16.overview: Tuberculosis is an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This entry is used when TB is diagnosed clinically without bacteriological confirmation — the clinical picture strongly suggests TB. Treatment follows the same 6-month regimen as confirmed TB.
phases: Intensive phase (Months 1–2) — RHZE daily
Continuation phase (Months 3–6) — RH daily
Completion — clinical resolution at month 6

medications.name: RHZE — Rifampicin + Isoniazid + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol
medications.notes: The 4-in-1 tablet. Take all tablets in ONE dose. Rifampicin may turn urine orange — harmless.

medications.name: RH — Rifampicin + Isoniazid
medications.notes: Two formulations: RH 150/75 mg and RH 300/150 mg.

medications.name: Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
medications.notes: Prevents isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy.

lifestyleAdvice: Take all your TB tablets every day without missing any dose
Do not stop treatment even if you feel better
Cover your mouth when you cough or sneeze
Open windows and let in sunlight at home
Eat a nutritious, balanced diet
Stop smoking and avoid excessive alcohol
Inform close contacts so they can be screened
Report immediately: yellow eyes/skin, dark urine, severe nausea, tingling, skin rash
A16.followUpSchedule: Monthly clinical review. Sputum smear at month 2, 5, 6. Response to treatment is the main confirmation of diagnosis.
warningSigns: New skin rash with fever or facial swelling
referralCriteria: Failure to improve after 2 months despite adherence

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Signs of disseminated TB, TB meningitis, or severe adverse drug reaction
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Refer to hospital same day. STOP all TB medicines if suspected hepatitis before referral.

specialCases.note: Start TB first, then add ART based on CD4. Double DTG dose while on rifampicin.
All first-line TB drugs are safe. Give pyridoxine daily.
Stop all TB medicines, refer urgently.

A16.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 17, Sections 17.4.1 and 17.4.1.2

J45.overview: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways. Exposure to triggers causes inflammation, bronchospasm, and increased mucus production, leading to episodes of wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough — especially at night or early morning. Asthma cannot be cured, but it can be well-controlled with regular treatment. Most treatment failures are due to poor inhaler technique or poor adherence.
J45.treatmentDurationText: Lifelong management — controlled with regular treatment

severityLevels.systolic: Symptoms <2× per month; no exacerbations in last 12 months
severityLevels.diastolic: Salbutamol as needed + low-dose ICS with each dose

severityLevels.systolic: Symptoms or reliever need ≥2× per month; any exacerbations
Symptoms most days; waking at night ≥1× per week
severityLevels.diastolic: High-dose ICS + reliever; escalate to LABA/ICS if uncontrolled

phases: Step 1 — Reliever + low-dose ICS with each reliever dose (mild asthma)
Step 2 — Daily low-dose ICS controller + reliever as needed (moderate asthma)
Step 3 — High-dose daily ICS + reliever; escalate to LABA/ICS combination if not controlled
Step-down — Only after 6 months of stability, taper slowly

medications.name: Salbutamol (Reliever / Rescue Inhaler)
medications.notes: Short-acting beta-2 agonist. Provides immediate relief. Increasing use means asthma is NOT controlled.

medications.name: Beclomethasone (Inhaled Corticosteroid — Controller)
medications.frequency: Step 1: 200 mcg with each salbutamol. Step 2: 200 mcg twice daily. Step 3: 400 mcg twice daily
medications.notes: Use every day even when well. Rinse mouth after each dose. Preferred ICS in patients on protease inhibitors (HIV).

medications.name: Budesonide (Inhaled Corticosteroid — Controller)
medications.frequency: Step 1: 200 mcg with each reliever. Step 2: 200 mcg twice daily. Step 3: 400 mcg twice daily
medications.notes: Alternative ICS. Interacts with protease inhibitors.

medications.name: Salmeterol/Fluticasone Combination (LABA/ICS)
medications.notes: Used when Step 3 ICS alone is not controlling symptoms.

lifestyleAdvice: Avoid triggers — dust, pollen, smoke, cold air
Stop smoking and avoid second-hand smoke
Keep pets out of the bedroom if pet dander triggers asthma
Wash bedding weekly in hot water
Use a spacer with your inhaler
Rinse mouth after using the preventer inhaler
Keep a reliever inhaler with you at all times
Track peak flow at home if you have a PEFR meter
Follow your asthma action plan
Get your annual flu vaccine
If symptoms wake you at night, your asthma is not controlled

baseline: PEFR improvement test (salbutamol 200 mcg → ≥20% or ≥60 L/min improvement)

J45.followUpSchedule: Review every 3 months. Step up if uncontrolled; step down slowly after 6 months. If >2 courses of oral prednisone in 6 months, refer to doctor.
warningSigns: Reliever needed more than 4 times a day
Waking up at night with cough or wheeze
Chest tightness not responding to reliever
Drowsiness or confusion during an attack
referralCriteria: >2 courses of oral prednisone within 6 months
Patients on protease inhibitors requiring inhaled fluticasone

emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: See J46 — Status asthmaticus for full protocol.

inhalerTechnique.mdi:
1. Remove cap and shake well.
2. Breathe out gently.
3. Seal lips around mouthpiece.
4. Press canister and breathe in slowly (3–5 sec).
5. Hold breath 10 sec.
6. Wait 30 sec between puffs.
7. Rinse mouth after steroid inhaler.
inhalerTechnique.spacer:
1. Shake inhaler, insert into spacer.
2. Seal lips around mouthpiece.
3. Press canister ONCE.
4. Breathe in and out slowly 5–6 times.
5. Wait 30 sec between puffs.
6. Wash spacer weekly, air-dry.
inhalerTechnique.nebulizer:
1. Assemble nebulizer, add medicine.
2. Sit upright, mouthpiece in mouth.
3. Turn on compressor.
4. Breathe normally until mist stops (5–10 min).
5. Wash after each use.
generalTips: Always shake the inhaler before use.
Use a spacer for ALL children and adults on Step 3.
Rinse mouth after using a preventer inhaler.
If using both reliever and preventer: reliever first, wait 5 min, then preventer.

specialCases.note: Diagnosis is difficult — refer all for assessment.
Use beclomethasone — budesonide and fluticasone interact with protease inhibitors.
Use reliever 15 minutes before exercise.
Continue asthma treatment — uncontrolled asthma is more dangerous.

J45.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 17, Section 17.1.3

J45.9.overview: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways. Exposure to triggers causes inflammation, bronchospasm, and increased mucus production, leading to episodes of wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and cough. This is the same condition as J45 — the code is used when the specific asthma subtype is not specified.

severityLevels.diastolic: Salbutamol as needed + low-dose ICS with each dose
High-dose ICS + reliever; escalate to LABA/ICS

phases: Step 1 — Reliever + low-dose ICS with each reliever dose
Step 2 — Daily low-dose ICS + reliever
Step 3 — High-dose ICS + reliever; escalate to LABA/ICS if uncontrolled

medications.name: Salbutamol (Reliever)
medications.notes: Immediate relief. Increasing use means asthma is NOT controlled.

medications.name: Beclomethasone (Controller)
medications.frequency: Step 2: 200 mcg twice daily. Step 3: 400 mcg twice daily
medications.notes: Use every day even when well. Rinse mouth after use.

medications.name: Budesonide (Controller)
medications.frequency: Step 2: 200 mcg twice daily. Step 3: 400 mcg twice daily
medications.notes: Alternative to beclomethasone. Interacts with protease inhibitors.

medications.name: Salmeterol/Fluticasone Combination (LABA/ICS)
medications.notes: Used when Step 3 ICS alone is not controlling.

lifestyleAdvice: Avoid triggers — dust, pollen, smoke, cold air
Stop smoking and avoid second-hand smoke
Use a spacer with your inhaler
Rinse mouth after using the preventer inhaler
Keep a reliever inhaler with you at all times
Get your annual flu vaccine
If symptoms wake you at night, your asthma is not controlled
J45.9.followUpSchedule: Review every 3 months. If >2 oral prednisone courses in 6 months, refer to doctor.
warningSigns: Reliever needed more than 4 times a day
Waking up at night with cough or wheeze
Chest tightness not responding to reliever
referralCriteria: >2 courses of oral prednisone within 6 months

inhalerTechnique.mdi:
1. Shake inhaler well.
2. Breathe out gently.
3. Seal lips around mouthpiece.
4. Press canister and breathe in slowly.
5. Hold breath 10 sec.
6. Rinse mouth after steroid inhaler.
inhalerTechnique.spacer:
1. Shake and insert inhaler.
2. Seal lips around mouthpiece.
3. Press canister ONCE.
4. Breathe in and out slowly 5–6 times.
5. Wash spacer weekly.
generalTips: Use a spacer for all children and Step 3 adults.

J45.9.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 17, Section 17.1.3

J46.overview: Status asthmaticus is a severe, life-threatening asthma attack that does not respond to usual reliever treatment. It is a medical emergency requiring immediate treatment and urgent referral. Patients present with severe breathlessness, inability to speak in full sentences, agitation, and often cyanosis. Early recognition and rapid treatment saves lives. Do NOT sedate the patient.
J46.treatmentDurationText: Acute emergency — refer after initial treatment

severityLevels.systolic: O2 sat >90%, talks in phrases, HR 100–120, PEFR >60%
severityLevels.diastolic: Salbutamol + spacer or nebulizer every 20–30 min + prednisone 40 mg

severityLevels.systolic: O2 sat <90%, talks in words, RR >30, HR >120, PEFR <60%
severityLevels.diastolic: Oxygen + salbutamol every 20–30 min + ipratropium + prednisone 40 mg — REFER

severityLevels.systolic: O2 sat <90%, unable to speak, drowsy, silent chest, PEFR <33%
severityLevels.diastolic: Oxygen + salbutamol + ipratropium × 4 doses + hydrocortisone IV 100 mg — REFER URGENTLY

phases: Step 1 — Assess severity (O2 sat, speech, HR, RR, PEFR)
Step 2 — Give oxygen to keep O2 sat 93–95%
Step 3 — Salbutamol by spacer OR nebulizer every 20–30 min
Step 4 — Add ipratropium if poor response
Step 5 — Give prednisone 40 mg (or hydrocortisone IV 100 mg)
Step 6 — Refer to hospital after initial treatment

medications.name: Salbutamol 100 mcg MDI
medications.frequency: Every 20–30 min for the first hour, then every 2–4 hours
medications.notes: Use with a spacer — as effective as nebulizer. Shake between each puff.

medications.name: Salbutamol 0.5% nebulizer solution
medications.dosage: 1 mL (5 mg) made up to 4 mL with sodium chloride 0.9%
medications.frequency: Every 20–30 min for the first hour, then every 2–4 hours
medications.notes: Deliver at 8 L/min with oxygen.

medications.name: Ipratropium bromide 0.5 mg/2 mL nebulizer solution
medications.frequency: Every 20–30 min up to 3 doses (severe attack)
medications.notes: For life-threatening attack: 4 doses over 2 hours.

medications.name: Prednisone (oral corticosteroid)
medications.notes: Give immediately. If unable to swallow, use hydrocortisone IV.

medications.name: Hydrocortisone (IV/IM corticosteroid)
medications.notes: Follow with oral prednisone 40 mg daily × 7 days.

medications.name: Oxygen
medications.notes: COPD patients: 24–28% Venturi mask, close monitoring.

lifestyleAdvice: Do NOT sedate the patient at any point
Sit the patient upright — do not lay them flat
Keep the patient calm
Do NOT give antibiotics routinely
After recovery, review: adherence, inhaler technique, trigger exposure
Warn the patient that asthma often flares again in the week after an attack
Refer patients with >2 oral prednisone courses in 6 months
J46.followUpSchedule: After an acute attack: review within 1–2 weeks. If >2 courses of oral steroids in 6 months, refer to doctor.
warningSigns: Unable to speak in full sentences
referralCriteria: All patients with severe or life-threatening attack
Lower threshold if: seen in afternoon/evening, recent nocturnal symptoms, previous severe attacks, rapid onset

emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Sit patient upright. Oxygen (93–95% target). Salbutamol 400–1000 mcg via spacer every 20–30 min. Add ipratropium if poor response. Give prednisone 40 mg (or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV). Continue treatment while arranging urgent referral. NEVER sedate.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Life-threatening — refer urgently after initial treatment.

specialCases.note: Treat the same, but give oxygen with care (24–28% Venturi mask). Add antibiotics ONLY if increased sputum purulence PLUS increased volume or dyspnoea.
In patients >50 years with first-time wheeze, consider pulmonary oedema due to LV failure.
Continue acute asthma management — treatment is the same.
AVOID sedation of any kind — critical.

J46.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 17, Section 17.1.1

A09.overview: A sudden onset of increased frequency of stools that are looser than normal, with or without vomiting. Commonly caused by a virus, but may be caused by bacteria or parasites. The cause cannot be diagnosed without laboratory investigation. Most cases are self-limiting and can be managed with rehydration. Dehydration is the main danger — especially in children.
A09.treatmentDurationText: Usually resolves in 3–7 days with correct rehydration
phases: Assess hydration status (Plan A: no dehydration / Plan B: some / Plan C: severe)
Rehydrate according to Plan A, B, or C
Zinc for children (10 mg daily × 14 days)
Continue feeding — do not starve the patient
Refer if severe dehydration, persistent diarrhoea, or danger signs

medications.name: Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)
medications.dosage: Plan B: 80 mL/kg over 4 hours (5 mL/kg every 15 min). Plan A: 10 mL/kg after each loose stool
medications.frequency: Frequent small sips from a cup and spoon
medications.notes: ORAL USE ONLY. Show caregiver how to give ORS with a cup and spoon using frequent small sips. If child vomits, wait 10 minutes and continue more slowly. Encourage continued feeding, especially breastfeeding.

medications.name: Homemade Sugar and Salt Solution (SSS)
medications.dosage: ½ level teaspoon table salt + 8 level teaspoons sugar in 1 litre of boiled (or clean) water
medications.frequency: As needed for rehydration at home
medications.notes: 1 level medicine measure ≈ 1 level 5 mL teaspoon. Use for home prevention of dehydration. Discard after 24 hours and make fresh.

medications.name: Zinc (elemental) — for children
medications.notes: Give zinc to ALL children with acute diarrhoea. Reduces duration and severity of diarrhoea and prevents future episodes.

medications.name: Loperamide — for adults
medications.dosage: 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool
medications.notes: Maximum daily dose depends on weight — see table below. NOT for children. NOT for bloody diarrhoea or suspected dysentery.

medications.name: Ceftriaxone (only before referral)
medications.phase: Neonates with severe dehydration OR children with SAM + severe dehydration or shock
medications.notes: Do NOT give routinely. Give ONLY to: neonates with severe dehydration, or children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) who have severe dehydration or shock. Avoid calcium-containing IV fluids with ceftriaxone in neonates. For IM: do not inject >1 g at one site.

lifestyleAdvice: Keep giving ORS or SSS even if the patient vomits — wait 10 minutes and continue slowly
Continue feeding — do NOT starve the patient. Breastfeed more frequently
Give small frequent meals at least 6 times a day
Give zinc to children every day for 14 days — do not stop early
Wash hands with soap after using the toilet and before preparing food
Boil drinking water if unsure of its safety
Wash all fruits and vegetables before eating
Keep food covered to prevent contamination by flies
Use a clean latrine or toilet — dispose of stools safely
Return to the clinic IMMEDIATELY if any warning signs appear
Come back for a follow-up visit in 5 days if diarrhoea has not stopped

duringEpisode: Assess hydration status at each contact
Check ability to drink and feed
Check for danger signs — sunken eyes, slow skin pinch, lethargy

A09.followUpSchedule: Return immediately if: condition does not improve, poor drinking or feeding, blood in stool, fever, sunken eyes, slow skin pinch. Follow-up in 5 days if diarrhoea persists.
warningSigns: Not able to drink or drinks poorly
referralCriteria: Severe dehydration (Plan C) — refer urgently after starting IV fluids
Failure to maintain hydration with oral fluids after Plan B (Some dehydration)
General danger signs: convulsions, altered consciousness, inability to feed
Dysentery in children <12 months of age or with dehydration
Suspected acute abdomen or surgical problem

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Severe dehydration (Plan C) — lethargy, sunken eyes, unable to drink, very slow skin pinch
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Ringers lactate or sodium chloride 0.9% IV, 20 mL/kg rapidly. If SAM: reduce to 10 mL/kg over 10 minutes. Repeat up to twice if weak radial pulse. Continue 20 mL/kg every hour for 5 hours while arranging urgent referral. Give ORS 5 mL/kg/hour as soon as the child can drink. If IV not possible, insert NG tube and give ORS 20 mL/kg/hour.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Life-threatening — refer urgently while continuing rehydration.

specialCases.note: Consider dysentery — refer. Dysentery in children <12 months requires hospital referral.

specialCases.case: High fever or very ill child
specialCases.note: Consider typhoid — refer.
See K52.9 — persistent diarrhoea. Give Vitamin A + zinc, review feeding, follow up in 5 days.
Consider cholera — refer immediately for isolation and treatment.
Give ceftriaxone IM/IV 100 mg/kg single dose BEFORE referral. Avoid calcium-containing IV fluids.
Reduce IV fluid bolus to 10 mL/kg over 10 minutes. Give ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg before referral.
Give zinc 10 mg daily for 14 days — do not stop early. Give with ORS at each loose stool.

A09.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 2, Sections 2.9.1 and 2.9.3

A09.9.conditionName: Gastroenteritis and colitis of unspecified origin
A09.9.overview: A sudden onset of increased frequency of stools that are looser than normal, with or without vomiting. This entry is used when the specific cause of gastroenteritis is not specified. Most cases are self-limiting and can be managed with rehydration. Dehydration is the main danger — especially in children.
A09.9.treatmentDurationText: Usually resolves in 3–7 days with correct rehydration
phases: Assess hydration status (Plan A: no dehydration / Plan B: some / Plan C: severe)
Rehydrate according to Plan A, B, or C
Zinc for children (10 mg daily × 14 days)
Continue feeding
Refer if severe dehydration, persistent diarrhoea, or danger signs

medications.name: Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)
medications.dosage: Plan B: 80 mL/kg over 4 hours. Plan A: 10 mL/kg after each loose stool
medications.notes: Show caregiver how to give with a cup and spoon. If child vomits, wait 10 min and continue more slowly.

medications.name: Homemade Sugar and Salt Solution (SSS)
medications.dosage: ½ level teaspoon salt + 8 level teaspoons sugar in 1 L boiled/cooled water
medications.notes: Discard after 24 hours and make fresh.

medications.name: Zinc — for children
medications.notes: Give zinc to ALL children with acute diarrhoea.

medications.name: Loperamide — for adults
medications.dosage: 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each loose stool
medications.notes: NOT for children. NOT for bloody diarrhoea.

medications.name: Ceftriaxone (only before referral)
medications.phase: Neonates with severe dehydration OR children with SAM + severe dehydration
medications.notes: Only before referral in specific high-risk groups. Avoid calcium-containing IV fluids in neonates.

lifestyleAdvice: Keep giving ORS or SSS even if the patient vomits
Continue feeding — do NOT starve the patient
Give small frequent meals 6× a day
Give zinc to children for 14 full days
Wash hands with soap after toilet and before food
Boil drinking water if unsure of safety
Wash fruits and vegetables before eating
Keep food covered
Return IMMEDIATELY if warning signs appear
Follow up in 5 days if diarrhoea persists

duringEpisode: Check ability to drink and feed

A09.9.followUpSchedule: Return immediately if: no improvement, poor drinking/feeding, blood in stool, fever, sunken eyes, slow skin pinch. Follow up in 5 days if diarrhoea persists.
referralCriteria: Failure of Plan B after 8 hours
Dysentery in children <12 months or with dehydration

emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Ringers lactate or sodium chloride 0.9% IV, 20 mL/kg rapidly. Repeat up to twice if weak pulse. Continue 20 mL/kg hourly × 5 hours. Give ORS as soon as child can drink. Refer urgently.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Life-threatening — refer urgently while continuing rehydration.

specialCases.note: Consider dysentery — refer.
Give ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg single dose before referral.
Reduce IV bolus to 10 mL/kg over 10 minutes. Give ceftriaxone before referral.
See K52.9 for persistent diarrhoea.

A09.9.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 2, Sections 2.9.1 and 2.9.3

K52.9.overview: Diarrhoea lasting 7–14 days in children, or >4 weeks in adults. In children, persistent diarrhoea often follows an acute episode and can lead to malnutrition. In adults, it may be a sign of underlying HIV or giardiasis. Management focuses on rehydration, nutritional support, and treating the underlying cause.
K52.9.treatmentDurationText: Variable — depends on cause; usually 1–4 weeks
phases: Assess for underlying cause — HIV, giardiasis, other infection
Rehydrate — prevent and treat dehydration
Nutritional support — especially in children
Specific treatment based on cause
Follow up in 5 days

medications.name: Vitamin A (retinol) — for children
medications.frequency: Single dose (may repeat if vomited immediately)
medications.notes: Cut the narrow end of the capsule with scissors. Open the child's mouth by gently squeezing the cheeks. Squeeze drops directly into the back of the mouth. Do NOT give the capsule to the caregiver. If the child spits up most of the liquid immediately, give one more dose.

weightBands.dose: 200,000 IU (1 capsule of 200,000 IU OR 2 capsules of 100,000 IU)

medications.name: Zinc (elemental)
medications.notes: Give to all children with persistent diarrhoea.

medications.name: Metronidazole — for adults (giardiasis)
medications.phase: Empiric treatment for giardiasis in adults
medications.notes: Empiric treatment is recommended before referring adults with chronic diarrhoea. Avoid alcohol during treatment — can cause a disulfiram-like reaction.

medications.name: Nutritional rehabilitation
medications.dosage: Small frequent meals — at least 6 times a day
medications.notes: If breastfeeding, give more frequent longer feeds. If replacement feeding, use fermented milk (amasi/maas) or yoghurt if available. Continue solids throughout.

lifestyleAdvice: If breastfeeding, give more frequent, longer feeds
If replacement feeding, use fermented milk (amasi) or yoghurt
Continue solids — give small frequent meals at least 6 times a day
Prevent dehydration with homemade sugar and salt solution (SSS)
Encourage HIV testing — most chronic diarrhoea in adults is HIV-related
Avoid alcohol while taking metronidazole
Wash hands with soap frequently
Boil drinking water if unsure of safety

baseline: Stool sample for ova, cysts, parasites (adults)

K52.9.followUpSchedule: Follow up in 5 days. If diarrhoea persists, refer to doctor.
warningSigns: Failure to gain weight in children
referralCriteria: All HIV-negative adults with no pathogen identified and significant diarrhoea

specialCases.note: See B20 — HIV-associated diarrhoea. Start ART.
Empiric treatment with metronidazole 2 g daily × 3 days is recommended before referring adults with chronic diarrhoea.
Give Vitamin A as a single dose to children with persistent diarrhoea. Follow the weight/age-band dosing above.

K52.9.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 2, Sections 2.9.2 and 2.9.4
